# Project Summary

# Set-Up Chunks

## Loading packages

```{r}
# Standard data manipulation/visualization and data loading packages
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

# Mixed effect model packages
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)

# Estimated marginal means for post-hoc testing
library(emmeans)
```

## Loading data sets

```{r}
# Saving Excel data to variables with read_excel
Height_Data_Raw = read_excel(
  "Oak Data Entry MCRS Field Trip.xlsx", 
  sheet = "Seedling Heights"
  )

Moist_Data_Raw = read_excel(
  "Oak Data Entry MCRS Field Trip.xlsx", 
  sheet = "Soil Moisture"
  )

SPAD_Data_Raw = read_excel(
  "Oak Data Entry MCRS Field Trip.xlsx", 
   sheet = "SPAD", na = "NA")
```

# 1. Cleaning Data with dplyr

## 1.1. Cleaning SPAD Data

```{r}
# Visual check to see if data looks as expected
SPAD_Data_Raw

# Cleaning SPAD data
SPAD_Data_Clean = SPAD_Data_Raw |>
  
  # Filtering out NA rows (there's a billion for some reason) with filter()
  filter(is.na(Treatment) == FALSE) |>
  
  # Removing NR treatment from our data with filter()
  filter(Treatment != "NR") |>
  
  # Creating new column for sapling number with separate()
  separate(Tag_Num,
    c("Tag_Num", "Sapling_Num"), 
    3, extra = "merge", fill = "right"
  ) |>
  
  # Converting Sapling_Num into characters and adding NA values where applicable
  # with mutate() and case_when()
  mutate(Sapling_Num = case_when(
    Sapling_Num == "A1" ~ "A",
    Sapling_Num == "A2" ~ "B",
    Sapling_Num == "A3" ~ "C",
    Sapling_Num == "" ~ NA,
    is.character(Sapling_Num) == TRUE ~ Sapling_Num
    )
  ) |>
  
  # Converting Sapling_Num to factor with mutate()
  mutate(Sapling_Num = as.factor(Sapling_Num)) |>
  
  # Adding indicator for multiple saplings for future use with mutate()
  mutate(Multiple_Seedling = case_when(
    is.na(Sapling_Num) == FALSE ~ TRUE,
    is.na(Sapling_Num) == TRUE ~ FALSE
    ),
    .after = Sapling_Num
  ) |>
  
  # Turning Multiple_Seedling into a factor with mutate()
  mutate(Multiple_Seedling = as.factor(Multiple_Seedling))
  
# Visual verification
SPAD_Data_Clean

# Removing QAQC columns to the right of Notes by identifying its column number with which() and then selecting only the columns to the left
Notes_colnum_SPAD = which(colnames(SPAD_Data_Clean) == "Notes")
SPAD_Data_Clean = SPAD_Data_Clean[1:Notes_colnum_SPAD]

# Visual verification
SPAD_Data_Clean

# Creating column of unique identifier numbers with mutate()
SPAD_Data_Clean = SPAD_Data_Clean |>
  mutate(ID_num = row_number(), .before = Notes)

# Visual verification
SPAD_Data_Clean

# Converting Leaf columns into Leaf_Num column with pivot_longer()
SPAD_Data_Clean = SPAD_Data_Clean |>
  pivot_longer(names_to = "Leaf_Num", values_to = "SPAD_Value", cols = 10:15) |>
  
  # Removing "Leaf" from Leaf_Num with separate()
  separate(Leaf_Num,
    c("Leaf", "Leaf_Num"), 
    4, extra = "merge", fill = "left"
  ) |>
  
  # Removing Leaf with select()
  select(-Leaf)

# Visual verification
SPAD_Data_Clean

# Blanket fix for each data type that's wrong with mutate()
SPAD_Data_Clean = SPAD_Data_Clean |>
  mutate(Tag_Num = as.integer(Tag_Num)) |>
  mutate(Num_leaves = as.integer(Num_leaves)) |>
  mutate(Leaf_Num = as.integer(Leaf_Num)) |>
  mutate(Date = as.character(Date))

# Visual verification
SPAD_Data_Clean
```

## 1.2. Cleaning Soil Moisture Data

```{r}
# Visual check to see if data looks as expected
Moist_Data_Raw

# Cleaning soil moisture data
Moist_Data_Clean = Moist_Data_Raw |> 
  
  # Removing excess NA rows with filter()
  filter(is.na(Treatment) == FALSE) |>
  
  # Removing NR treatment from our data with filter()
  filter(Treatment != "NR") |>
  
  # Changing "NA" to actual native NA value with mutate() and case_when()
  mutate(VWC1_perc = case_when(
    VWC1_perc == "NA" ~ NA,
    VWC1_perc != "NA" ~ VWC1_perc
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(PER1_ms = case_when(
    PER1_ms == "NA" ~ NA,
    PER1_ms != "NA" ~ PER1_ms
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(VWC2_perc = case_when(
    VWC2_perc == "NA" ~ NA,
    VWC2_perc != "NA" ~ VWC2_perc
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(PER2_ms = case_when(
    PER2_ms == "NA" ~ NA,
    PER2_ms != "NA" ~ PER2_ms
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(VWC3_perc = case_when(
    VWC3_perc == "NA" ~ NA,
    VWC3_perc != "NA" ~ VWC3_perc
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(PER3_ms = case_when(
    PER3_ms == "NA" ~ NA,
    PER3_ms != "NA" ~ PER3_ms
    )
  )

# Visual verification
Moist_Data_Clean

# Removing QAQC columns to the right of Notes by identifying its column number with which() and then selecting only the columns to the left
Notes_colnum_Moist = which(colnames(Moist_Data_Clean) == "Notes")
Moist_Data_Clean = Moist_Data_Clean[1:Notes_colnum_Moist]

# Visual verification
Moist_Data_Clean

# Creating column of unique identifier numbers with mutate()
Moist_Data_Clean = Moist_Data_Clean |>
  mutate(ID_num = row_number())

# Visual verification
Moist_Data_Clean

# Converting VWC/PER columns into VWC_or_PER and value columns with pivot_longer()
Moist_Data_Clean = Moist_Data_Clean |>
  pivot_longer(names_to = "VWC_or_PER", values_to = "value", cols = 6:11) |>
  
  # Removing tail end of name from VWC_or_PER with separate()
  separate(VWC_or_PER,
    c("VWC_or_PER", "type"), "_"
  ) |>
  
  # Separating VWC_or_PER again with separate() to create a new measure_num
  # column
  separate(VWC_or_PER,
    c("VWC_or_PER", "measure_num"),
    3, extra = "merge", fill = "right"
  ) |>
  
  # Removing type and ID_num columns with select()
  select(-type, -ID_num) |>
  
  # Removing NA values with filter()
  filter(is.na(value) == FALSE)

# Visual verification
Moist_Data_Clean

# Blanket fixing data types with mutate()
Moist_Data_Clean = Moist_Data_Clean |>
  mutate(measure_num = as.integer(measure_num)) |>
  mutate(value = as.double(value)) |>
  mutate(Date = as.character(Date))

# Visual verification
Moist_Data_Clean
```

## 1.3. Cleaning Height Data

```{r}
# Visual check to see if data looks as expected
Height_Data_Raw
  
# Cleaning Height_Data
Height_Data_Clean = Height_Data_Raw |>
  
  # Remove NA rows
  filter(is.na(Treatment) == FALSE) |>
  
  # Removing NR treatment from our data with filter()
  filter(Treatment != "NR") |>
  
  # Changing alphanumeric Sapling_AB_etc values to characters
  mutate(Sapling_AB_etc = case_when(
    Sapling_AB_etc == "A1" ~ "A",
    Sapling_AB_etc == "A2" ~ "B",
    Sapling_AB_etc == "A3" ~ "C",
    is.na(Sapling_AB_etc) == TRUE ~ NA
    )
  ) |>
  
  # Adding indicator for multiple saplings for future use with mutate()
  mutate(Multiple_Seedling = case_when(
    is.na(Sapling_AB_etc) == FALSE ~ TRUE,
    is.na(Sapling_AB_etc) == TRUE ~ FALSE
  ),
  .after = Sapling_AB_etc
  ) |>
  
  # Turning Multiple_Seedling into a factor with mutate()
  mutate(Multiple_Seedling = as.factor(Multiple_Seedling)) |>
  
  # Removing that one random NA value in Dead_Alive
  filter(is.na(Dead_Alive) == FALSE) |>
  
  # Removing any treatment IDs that are incorrect
  filter(Treatment %in% c("AC", "DT", "OS"))

# Visual verification
Height_Data_Clean

# Removing QAQC data
Notes_colnum_Height = which(colnames(Height_Data_Clean) == "Notes")
Height_Data_Clean = Height_Data_Clean[1:Notes_colnum_Height]

# Visual verification
Height_Data_Clean

# Blanket fixing data types with mutate()
Height_Data_Clean = Height_Data_Clean |>
  mutate(Tag_Num = as.integer(Tag_Num)) |>
  mutate(Date = as.character(Date))

# Visual verification
Height_Data_Clean

# Editing in missing Sapling_AB_etc data with mutate() and replace(). I'm doing this manually because trying to select for randomly distributed values in a column sucks.
Height_Data_Clean = Height_Data_Clean |>
  mutate(Sapling_AB_etc = replace(Sapling_AB_etc, 1, "A")) |>
  mutate(Sapling_AB_etc = replace(Sapling_AB_etc, 2, "B")) |>
  mutate(Sapling_AB_etc = replace(Sapling_AB_etc, 10, "B")) |>
  mutate(Sapling_AB_etc = replace(Sapling_AB_etc, 11, "A")) |>
  mutate(Sapling_AB_etc = replace(Sapling_AB_etc, 29, "A")) |>
  mutate(Sapling_AB_etc = replace(Sapling_AB_etc, 30, "B")) |>
  mutate(Sapling_AB_etc = replace(Sapling_AB_etc, 31, "C")) |>
  
  # Repeating call creating indicator for multiple saplings with mutate()
  mutate(Multiple_Seedling = case_when(
    is.na(Sapling_AB_etc) == FALSE ~ TRUE,
    is.na(Sapling_AB_etc) == TRUE ~ FALSE
    )
  )

# Visual verification
Height_Data_Clean
```

# 2. Statistical Analysis

We want to establish that the storm that occurred did not modify any relationships in our measurements. As such, we will conduct regressions for SPAD value, seedling height, and leaf count with volumetric water content as the predictor for before and after the storm.

## 2.1. Evaluating VWC by Day

#### Initial Visualization of VWC by Day

```{r}
# Visualizing mean VWC by Day
Moist_Data_Clean |> 
  
  # Grouping days into before and after the storm with mutate() and case_when()
  mutate(Day = case_when(
    Date == "2026-10-08" ~ 1,
    Date != "2026-10-08" ~ 2
    )
  ) |>
  
  # Converting Day into a factor with mutate()
  mutate(Day = as.factor(Day)) |>
  
  # Selecting VWC measurements only with filter()
  filter(VWC_or_PER == "VWC") |>
  
  # Generating summary statistics with summarise()
  group_by(Day) |>
  summarise(
    mean_VWC = mean(value),
    sd_VWC = sd(value),
    n = n(),
    se_VWC = sd_VWC/sqrt(n)
  ) |>
  
  # Generating column plot with errorbars using ggplot() + geom_col() +
  # geom_errorbar()
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = Day, y = mean_VWC) +
  geom_col(color = "black", fill = NA) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(
    ymin = mean_VWC - se_VWC,
    ymax = mean_VWC + se_VWC
    ),
    position = position_dodge(0.9), width = 0.2
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = 12, family = "serif"),
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Day",
    y = "Volumetric Water Content (as a percentage)"
  )
```

Column plot of mean VWC on each sampling day, before and after the storm. Standard error bars are visualized at the top of each column. There appears to be a very large difference between the soil volumetric water content between the two days, consistent with the expected impact from the storm.

#### Checking Prerequisites for ANOVA Testing

```{r}
# Creating copies of Moist_Data_Clean for each day
Moist_Day_ANOVA = Moist_Data_Clean |>
    
  # Grouping days into before and after the storm with mutate() and
  # case_when() 
  mutate(Day = case_when(
    Date == "2026-10-08" ~ 1,
    Date != "2026-10-08" ~ 2
    ),
    .before = Team
  ) |>
  
  # Converting Day into a factor with mutate()
  mutate(Day = as.factor(Day)) |>
  
  # Removing Date column with select()
  select(-Date) |>
  
  # Selecting VWC measurements only with filter()
  filter(VWC_or_PER == "VWC")

# Creating mixed effect models for VWC ~ Day with lmer(), with Treatment and Block as random effects
Moist_Day_Model = lmer(value ~ Day + (1|Treatment) + (1|Block),
  data = Moist_Day_ANOVA)

# Checking plot of residuals vs. fitted for our models with plot()
plot(Moist_Day_Model)
```

Our model clearly does not exhibit homogeneity of variance. We'll investigate the data to check for outliers.

```{r}
# Checking data for outliers
Moist_Day_ANOVA
```

We have no outliers that are valid to remove, so we will compare sample sizes between treatments to see if they are comparable.

```{r}
# Generating counts of values for each treatment with summarise()
Moist_Day_ANOVA |>
  group_by(Treatment) |>
  summarise(n = n())
```

Our overall sample size is large and sample sizes for the individual treatments are comparable, so we will assume that the anova() function is robust enough to handle the heteroskedasticity.

```{r}
# Checking for normality in VWC with hist()
hist(Moist_Day_ANOVA$value)
```

Our data is not normally distributed, but we can assume normality since our sample size is large enough for the central limit theorem to apply (n = 78).

#### Conducting ANOVA Test

```{r}
# Displaying ANOVA table with anova()
VWC_ANOVA = anova(Moist_Day_Model)
VWC_ANOVA

# Saving ANOVA table with write.csv()
write.csv(VWC_ANOVA, "VWC_ANOVA.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

Results of a multiple-effects ANOVA with the form VWC \~ Day return a p-value lower than 2e-16, suggesting that there is a difference in soil volumetric water content before and after the storm.

#### Visualizing ANOVA Results

```{r}
# Generating visual of mean VWC by Day, with error bars and ANOVA results included
Moist_Day_ANOVA |>
  
  # Generating summary statistics with summarise()
  group_by(Day) |>
  summarise(
    mean_VWC = mean(value),
    sd_VWC = sd(value),
    n = n(),
    se_VWC = sd_VWC/sqrt(n)
  ) |>
  
  # Generating column plot with errorbars using ggplot() + geom_col() +
  # geom_errorbar()
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = Day, y = mean_VWC) +
  geom_col(color = "black", fill = NA) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(
    ymin = mean_VWC - se_VWC,
    ymax = mean_VWC + se_VWC
  ),

  ) +

# Saving plot with ggsave()
ggsave("VWC_ANOVA_Plot.png", path = "Plots", units = "in", width = 5.5,

```

Column plot of mean volumetric water content in soils between sampling days, with standard error bars depicted at the top of each column. A mixed-effects ANOVA showed a strong significant difference in VWC between the two days; results are denoted on the individual columns.

## 2.2. Regression Testing with SPAD_Value \~ VWC

#### Combining SPAD and Soil Moisture Data

```{r}
# Cleaning up soil moisture data more to prep it for combination
Moist_condensed = Moist_Data_Clean |>
  
  # Removing PER measurements with filter()
  filter(VWC_or_PER == "VWC") |>
  
  # Condensing VWC measurements to an average of the three measurements with
  # summarise()
  group_by(Treatment, Block) |>
  mutate(
    VWC = mean(as.double(value), na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  
  # Removing excess columns with select()
  select(-VWC_or_PER, -measure_num, -value, -Team, -Entered_By) |>
  
  # Removing duplicate rows with distinct()
  distinct(VWC, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  
  # Removing Block 4 Natural Recruits due to them having no data
  filter(is.na(VWC) == FALSE) |>
  
  # Creating join-friendly date column by editing dates with mutate()
  mutate(Day = case_when(
    Date == "2026-10-08" ~ "1",
    Date != "2026-10-08" ~ "2"
  ),
  .before = Block
  ) |>
  
  # Swapping new date column to a Factor with mutate()
  mutate(Day = as.factor(Day)) |>
  
  # Removing Date column with select()
  select(-Date)

# Visual verification
Moist_condensed

# Cleaning up SPAD data more to prep it for combination
SPAD_condensed = SPAD_Data_Clean |>
  
  # Removing Leaf_Num with select() so it doesn't complicate our math
  select(-Leaf_Num) |>
  
  # Removing excess metadata columns with select()
  select(-Team, -Entered_By) |>
  
  # Taking mean SPAD value per plant with mutate()
  group_by(ID_num, Sapling_Num) |>
  mutate(SPAD_Value = mean(SPAD_Value, na.rm = TRUE, .before = ID_num)) |>
  
  # Removing duplicate rows with distinct()
  distinct(SPAD_Value, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  
  # Creating join-friendly date column by editing dates with mutate()
  mutate(Day = case_when(
    Date == "2026-10-08" ~ "1",
    Date != "2026-10-08" ~ "2"
  ),
  .before = Block
  ) |>
  
  # Swapping new date column to a Factor with mutate()
  mutate(Day = as.factor(Day)) |>
  
  # Removing Date column with select()
  select(-Date)

# Visual verification
SPAD_condensed

# Combining tibbles with left_join() to blend identical columns
SPAD_Moist_combined = left_join(SPAD_condensed, Moist_condensed,
  join_by(Block, Treatment, Day)
  )

# Visual verification
SPAD_Moist_combined

# Removing NA values with filter()
SPAD_Moist_combined = SPAD_Moist_combined |>
  filter(is.na(VWC) == FALSE) |>
  filter(is.na(SPAD_Value) == FALSE)

# Visual verification
SPAD_Moist_combined
```

#### Initial Visualization of SPAD_Value \~ VWC

Since there was a rainstorm between the two sampling days, we'll be faceting all graphs by Day to ensure this doesn't impact our visualizations.

```{r}
# Generating scatter plot with a best-fit line using ggplot() + geom_point() + geom_smooth(), faceted with facet_wrap()
SPAD_Moist_combined |> ggplot() +
  aes(x = VWC, y = SPAD_Value) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black", linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~Day, scales = "free_x") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = 12, family = "serif")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Volumetric Water Content (as a percentage)",
    y = "SPAD value"
  )
```

There are several outlier data points at the bottom of the graph. We will investigate our data to see why this is occurring.

```{r}
# Visualizing data to identify outliers
SPAD_Moist_combined

# Removing outliers with filter()
SPAD_Moist_combined = SPAD_Moist_combined |>
  filter(Num_leaves != 0)

# Visual verification
SPAD_Moist_combined
```

The lower outlier points were SPAD values taken from dead plants. With those removed, we will re-visualize our data.

```{r}
SPAD_Moist_combined |> ggplot() +
  aes(x = VWC, y = SPAD_Value) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black", linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~Day, scales = "free_x",
    labeller = labeller(
      Day = c("1" = "Day 1", "2" = "Day 2")
    )
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = 12, family = "serif"),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 12, family = "serif"),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = NA, color = NA)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Volumetric Water Content (as a percentage)",
    y = "SPAD Value (in SPADs)"
  )
```

Scatter plot of SPAD value as a function of volumetric water content, faceted by sampling day. While volumetric water content does increase between the two days due to the storm the relationship with SPAD value appears approximately the same, exhibiting an extremely weak positive relationship. This likely indicates that volumetric water content alone is not the primary determinant of SPAD value.

#### Checking Prerequisites for a Linear Regression

```{r}
# Splitting the combined data into two separate tibbles by Day using filter()
SPAD_Moist_Day1 = SPAD_Moist_combined |>
  filter(Day == 1)

SPAD_Moist_Day2 = SPAD_Moist_combined |>
  filter(Day == 2)

# Visual verification
SPAD_Moist_Day1
SPAD_Moist_Day2

# Creating mixed effect models for each Day using lmer() with Treatment, Multiple_Seedling, and Block as random effects
SPAD_Moist_Day1_Model = lmer(
  SPAD_Value ~ VWC + (1|Treatment) + (1|Multiple_Seedling) + (1|Block),
  data = SPAD_Moist_Day1)

SPAD_Moist_Day2_Model = lmer(
  SPAD_Value ~ VWC + (1|Treatment) + (1|Multiple_Seedling) + (1|Block),
  data = SPAD_Moist_Day2)

# Checking residuals vs. fitted plot for our models with plot()
plot(SPAD_Moist_Day1_Model)
plot(SPAD_Moist_Day2_Model)

# Checking normality of SPAD_Value with hist()
hist(x = SPAD_Moist_Day1$SPAD_Value)
hist(x = SPAD_Moist_Day2$SPAD_Value)
```

Our data do both exhibit sufficient homogeneity of variance, but neither appear to exhibit clear normality. We will test a log-transformation on both models.

```{r}
# Creating mixed effect models for each Day using lmer() with Treatment, Multiple_Seedling, and Block as random effects
SPAD_Moist_Day1_Model_log = lmer(
  log(SPAD_Value) ~ log(VWC) + (1|Treatment) + (1|Multiple_Seedling) +
  (1|Block), data = SPAD_Moist_Day1)

SPAD_Moist_Day2_Model_log = lmer(
  log(SPAD_Value) ~ log(VWC) + (1|Treatment) + (1|Multiple_Seedling) +
  (1|Block), data = SPAD_Moist_Day2)

# Checking residuals vs. fitted plot for our models with plot()
plot(SPAD_Moist_Day1_Model_log)
plot(SPAD_Moist_Day2_Model_log)

# Checking normality of SPAD_Value with hist()
hist(log(SPAD_Moist_Day1$SPAD_Value), breaks = 10)
hist(log(SPAD_Moist_Day2$SPAD_Value), breaks = 18)
```

Our data still does not appear normal. We will conduct Shapiro-Wilk tests on our log-transformed models and compare these to the original models.

```{r}
# COnducting Shapiro-Wilk tests on our log models' residuals with shapiro.test()
shapiro.test(resid(SPAD_Moist_Day1_Model_log))
shapiro.test(resid(SPAD_Moist_Day2_Model_log))

# COnducting Shapiro-Wilk tests on our old models' residuals with shapiro.test()
shapiro.test(resid(SPAD_Moist_Day1_Model))
shapiro.test(resid(SPAD_Moist_Day2_Model))
```

Both our log models (p1 = 0.1717, p2 = 0.7348) and our original models (p1 = 0.1278, p2 = 0.8758) are suitable/normal according to these results, so we will use our original models for the sake of simplicity.

#### Conducting Regression Test

```{r}
# Reviewing summary of linear models with summary()
summary(SPAD_Moist_Day1_Model)
summary(SPAD_Moist_Day2_Model)
```

A model of SPAD value as a function of VWC with block integrated as a random effect and no interactions with treatment showed no significant relationship between the two measurements on either day (p1 = 0.42, p2 = 0.96). We thus cannot reject our null hypothesis and lack support for a relationship between the two values. At the very least, VWC does not appear to be a good predictor of SPAD value.

#### Visualizing Regression Results

```{r}
# Generating scatter plot for our data using ggplot() + geom_point(), faceted with facet_wrap()
SPAD_Moist_combined |> ggplot() +
  aes(x = VWC, y = SPAD_Value) +
  facet_wrap(~Day, scales = "free_x",
    labeller = labeller(
      Day = c("1" = "Day 1", "2" = "Day 2")
      )
    ) +
  geom_point() +

    x = 7.5, y = 45, size = 12, size.unit = "pt", family = "serif") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = 12, family = "serif"),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 12, family = "serif"),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = NA, color = NA)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Volumetric Water Content (as a percentage)",
    y = "SPAD Value (in SPADs)"
  )

# Saving plot with ggsave()
ggsave("SPAD_VWC_Regression_Plot.png", path = "Plots", units = "in", width = 5.5,
  height = 3.75, dpi = 300)
```

Scatter plot of SPAD value as a function of volumetric water content across all treatment types, faceted by sampling day. Results of a simple regression are displayed on the top left of each facet. There appears to be no relationship between SPAD value and volumetric water content, both before and after the rainstorm occurred.

## 2.3. Regression Testing with Leaf Count \~ VWC

#### Combining Leaf Count and Soil Moisture Data

We can reuse our cleaned data from the SPAD value \~ VWC regression, as that retained data on leaf count.

```{r}
# Visual verification
SPAD_condensed

# Cleaning data further to fit leaf count testing better
Leaf_condensed = SPAD_condensed |>
  
  # Preemptively removing NA SPAD values and leaf counts of 0 using filter() to fit
  # with previous cleaning done to SPAD data
  filter(is.na(SPAD_Value) == FALSE) |>
  filter(Num_leaves > 0) |>
  
  # Removing duplicated leaf count values with distinct()
  group_by(ID_num, Sapling_Num) |>
  distinct(Num_leaves, .keep_all = TRUE)

# Visual verification
Leaf_condensed

# Combining tibbles with left_join() to blend identical columns
Leaf_Moist_combined = left_join(Leaf_condensed, Moist_condensed,
  join_by(Block, Treatment, Day)
)

# Visual verification
Leaf_Moist_combined

# Removing NA values of VWC with filter()
Leaf_Moist_combined = Leaf_Moist_combined |>
  filter(is.na(VWC) == FALSE)

# Visual verification
Leaf_Moist_combined
```

#### Initial Visualization of Leaf Count \~ VWC

```{r}
# Creating scatter plot with a best-fit-line using ggplot() + geom_point() + geom_smooth(), faceted using facet_wrap()
Leaf_Moist_combined |> ggplot() +

    x = "Volumetric Water Content (as a percentage)",

```

This is clearly skewed by a large outlier. We will visually check our data to investigate why.

```{r}
# Visual check for outliers
Leaf_Moist_combined
```

The outlier is part of the open sky treatment but deviates so far from expectation we will still cut it, noting this in our final figure, and re-visualize our data.

```{r}
# Visual verification

Leaf_Moist_combined |> ggplot() +

  geom_point() +

```

Scatter plot of leaf count as a function of volumetric water count, faceted by sampling day. Visuals are heavily skewed by a few large data points. There appears to be a negative relationship between leaf count and volumetric water content before the storm and a weakly positive relationship after.

#### Checking Prerequisites for a Linear Regression

```{r}
# Splitting the combined data into two separate tibbles by Day using filter()
Leaf_Moist_Day1 = Leaf_Moist_combined |>
  filter(Day == 1)

Leaf_Moist_Day2 = Leaf_Moist_combined |>
  filter(Day == 2)

# Visual verification
Leaf_Moist_Day1
Leaf_Moist_Day2

# Creating mixed-effects models for each Day using lmer() with Treatment, Multiple_Seedling, and Block as random effects
Leaf_Moist_Day1_Model = lmer(
  Num_leaves ~ VWC + (1|Treatment) + (1|Multiple_Seedling) + (1|Block),
  data = Leaf_Moist_Day1)

Leaf_Moist_Day2_Model = lmer(
  Num_leaves ~ VWC + (1|Treatment) + (1|Multiple_Seedling) + (1|Block),
  data = Leaf_Moist_Day2)

# Viewing plot of residuals vs. fitted for our models with plot()
plot(Leaf_Moist_Day1_Model)
plot(Leaf_Moist_Day2_Model)

# Checking histogram of leaf count using hist()
hist(Leaf_Moist_Day1$Num_leaves, breaks = 16)
hist(Leaf_Moist_Day2$Num_leaves, breaks = 16)
```

Our data exhibit sufficient homogeneity of variance but are heavily skewed. We will test a log transformation for both.

```{r}
# Creating mixed-effects models for each Day using lmer() with Treatment, Multiple_Seedling, and Block as random effects with a log() transformation applied
Leaf_Moist_Day1_Model_log = lmer(
  log(Num_leaves) ~ log(VWC) + (1|Treatment) + (1|Multiple_Seedling) + (1|Block),
  data = Leaf_Moist_Day1)

Leaf_Moist_Day2_Model_log = lmer(
  log(Num_leaves) ~ log(VWC) + (1|Treatment) + (1|Multiple_Seedling) + (1|Block),
  data = Leaf_Moist_Day2)

# Viewing plot of residuals vs. fitted for our models with plot()
plot(Leaf_Moist_Day1_Model_log)
plot(Leaf_Moist_Day2_Model_log)

# Checking histogram of log leaf count using hist()
hist(log(Leaf_Moist_Day1$Num_leaves))
hist(log(Leaf_Moist_Day2$Num_leaves))
```

The log-transformed models both exhibit sufficient homogeneity of variance but still leave normality in question. We will conduct a Shapiro-Wilk test on each of our models' residuals and compare these to results for our original models.

```{r}
# Conducting Shapiro-Wilk test on our log models' residuals using shapiro.test()
shapiro.test(resid(Leaf_Moist_Day1_Model_log))
shapiro.test(resid(Leaf_Moist_Day2_Model_log))

# Conducting Shapiro-Wilk test on our inital models' residuals using shapiro.test()
shapiro.test(resid(Leaf_Moist_Day1_Model))
shapiro.test(resid(Leaf_Moist_Day2_Model))
```

The original model is best for the Day 1 data (p = 0.2887) and the log-transformed model is best for the Day 2 data (p = 0.4797), so we will select these and move on to our regression testing.

#### Conducting Simple Regression Test

```{r}
# Visualizing summary table of our models with summary()
summary(Leaf_Moist_Day1_Model)
summary(Leaf_Moist_Day2_Model_log)
```

A model of log leaf count as a function of log volumetric water content, with block, treatment, and multiple saplings integrated as random effects, showed no significant relationship between the two measurements on either day (p1 = 0.0773, p2 = 0.5495). We thus cannot reject our null hypothesis and lack support for a relationship between the two values.

#### Visualizing Regression Results

```{r}
  geom_text(
    label = c("p = 0.0773\nt = -1.877\ndf = 17.526"),

    ) +

Leaf_Moist_Day2_Plot = Leaf_Moist_Day2 |> ggplot() +
  aes(x = log(VWC), y = log(Num_leaves)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(
```

Scatter plot of leaf count as a function of volumetric water content across all treatment types, separated by sampling day. Day 2 data have been log-transformed. Results of a simple regression are displayed in the top left of each graph. There appears to be no relationship between leaf count and volumetric water content, both before and after the rainstorm occurred. While the p-value for the Day 1 data regression appears to be close to the threshold of 0.05, the low degrees of freedom for this test likely mean this number is misleading. *Note: An outlier seedling from the OS treatment with a leaf count of 112 was removed.*

## 2.4. Evaluating Survivorship by Treatment

#### Generating Tibble of Survival Rates by Treatment at each Block

```{r}
# Taking count of dead & living plants at each block
Survivor_Data = Height_Data_Clean |>
  
  # Generating summary table of counts with summarise()
  group_by(Treatment, Block, Dead_Alive) |>
  summarise(n = n()) |>
  
  # Generating a column recording the total number of plants with mutate()
  mutate(Total_Plants = sum(n)) |>
  
  # Pivoting the Dead_Alive column into separate columns with pivot_wider()
  pivot_wider(names_from = Dead_Alive, values_from = n) |>
  
  # Changing NA values of Dead and Alive to 0 using mutate()
  mutate(Alive = case_when(
    is.na(Alive) == TRUE ~ 0,
    is.na(Alive) == FALSE ~ Alive
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(Dead = case_when(
    is.na(Dead) == TRUE ~ 0,
    is.na(Dead) == FALSE ~ 0
    )
  ) |>
  
  # Taking survivorship as a percentage using mutate()
  mutate(Survival = Alive/Total_Plants)

# Visual verification
Survivor_Data

# Saving number of plots with multiple seedlings to a variable
Multiple_plots = Height_Data_Clean |>
  
  # Thinning MUltiple_Seedling data with distinct()
  group_by(Tag_Num) |>
  distinct(Multiple_Seedling, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  
  # Generating summary table of counts with summarise()
  group_by(Treatment, Block, Tag_Num, Multiple_Seedling) |>
  summarise(n = n()) |>
  
  # Selecting only the values with multiple seedlings using filter()
  ungroup() |>
  filter(Multiple_Seedling == TRUE) |>
  
  # Generating proportion of plots with multiple seedlings in overall plots using
  # mutate()
  mutate(
    Plot_Ratio = n/3
  ) |>
  
  # Removing excess columns with select()
  select(-Multiple_Seedling, -n) |>
  
  # Taking average proportion of plot with multiple seedlings in overall plots using
  # summarise()
  group_by(Treatment, Block) |>
  summarise(Mean_Plot_Ratio = mean(Plot_Ratio)) |>
  ungroup()

# Visual verification
Multiple_plots

# Joining the multiple seedling data onto the survivorship data with left_join()
Survivor_Data = left_join(Survivor_Data, Multiple_plots, join_by(
    Treatment, Block
    )
  )

# Visual verification
Survivor_Data

# Removing NA values from our new column with mutate()
Survivor_Data = Survivor_Data|>
  mutate(Mean_Plot_Ratio = case_when(
    is.na(Mean_Plot_Ratio) == TRUE ~ 0,
    is.na(Mean_Plot_Ratio) == FALSE ~ Mean_Plot_Ratio
    )
  )

# Visual verification
Survivor_Data
```

#### Initial Visualization of Survivorship by Treatment

```{r}
# Creating visualization of mean survivorship by treatment
Survivor_Data |>
  
  # Generating summary statistics with summarise()
  group_by(Treatment) |>
  summarise(
    mean_Survival = mean(Survival),
    sd_Survival = sd(Survival),
    n = n(),
    se_Survival = sd_Survival/sqrt(n) 
  ) |>
  
  # Creating column plot with error bars using ggplot() + geom_col() +
  # geom_errorbar()
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = Treatment, y = mean_Survival) +
  geom_col(color = "black", fill = NA) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(
      ymin = mean_Survival - se_Survival,
      ymax = mean_Survival + se_Survival
    ),
    width = 0.2, position = position_dodge(0.9)
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = 12, family = "serif"),
    legend.position =  "none",
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Treatment",
    y = "Survivorship (as a percentage)"
  )
```

Column plot of mean survivorship between treatments, with standard error bars visualized at the top of each column. It's difficult to determine if there are any true differences between treatments, as the columns appear different from one another but the large standard error means this visual could be misleading.

#### Checking Prerequisites for ANOVA Testing

```{r}
# Generating mixed-effects model for survivorship using lmer(), using Block, Total_Plants, and Mean_Plot_Ratio as random effects
Survivor_Model = lmer(Survival ~ Treatment + (1|Block) + (1|Total_Plants) +
  (1|Mean_Plot_Ratio), data = Survivor_Data)

# Checking plot of residuals vs. fitted for our model with plot()
plot(Survivor_Model)

# Checking histogram of survivorship with hist()
hist(Survivor_Data$Survival, breaks = 10)
```

Our data have homogeneity of variance but it is unclear if there is normality. We'll attempt a Shapiro-Wilk test on the residuals of our model.

```{r}
# Conducting Shapiro-Wilk test on our model's residuals using shapiro.test()
shapiro.test(resid(Survivor_Model))
```

A Shapiro-Wilk test confirms our data is normal (p = 0.9781), so we can continue with an ANOVA test.

#### Conducting ANOVA Test

```{r}
# Displaying ANOVA table with anova()
Survivor_ANOVA = anova(Survivor_Model)
Survivor_ANOVA

# Saving ANOVA table to CSV with write.csv()
write.csv(Survivor_ANOVA, "Survivor_ANOVA.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

Our ANOVA table shows no strongly significant differences found among treatments (p = 0.0851). Degrees of freedom are notably low.

#### Visualizing ANOVA Results

```{r}
# Creating visualization of mean survivorship by treatment
Survivor_Data |>
  
  # Generating summary statistics with summarise()
  group_by(Treatment) |>
  summarise(
    mean_Survival = mean(Survival),
    sd_Survival = sd(Survival),
    n = n(),
    se_Survival = sd_Survival/sqrt(n) 
  ) |>
  
  # Creating column plot with error bars using ggplot() + geom_col() +
  # geom_errorbar()
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = Treatment, y = mean_Survival) +
  geom_col(color = "black", fill = NA) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(
      ymin = mean_Survival - se_Survival,
      ymax = mean_Survival + se_Survival
    ),
    width = 0.2, position = position_dodge(0.9)
  ) +
  geom_text(label = c("A", "A", "A"),
    vjust = 5, size = 6, family = "serif"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    label = c("F = 2.8584\ndf1 = 2\ndf2 = 17\np = 0.0851"),
    x = 3, y = 0.6, size = 12, size.unit = "pt", family = "serif"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = 12, family = "serif"),
    legend.position =  "none",
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Treatment",
    y = "Survivorship (as a percentage)"
  )

# Saving plot with ggsave()
ggsave("Survivorship_ANOVA_Plot.png", path = "Plots", units = "in", width = 5.5, 
  height = 3.75, dpi = 300)
```

Column plot of mean survivorship between treatments, with standard error bars depicted at the top of each column. Results from a one-way ANOVA are denoted within each column. No strong significant differences were found between the three treatments. While the p-value for this test does appear to be close to the threshold of 0.05, the low degrees of freedom mean this number is likely misleading.

#### Checking Prerequisites for ANOVA Testing

```{r}
# Creating backup SPAD data set with no NAs for testing using filter()
SPAD_Data_no_NA = SPAD_Data_Clean |>
  filter(is.na(SPAD_Value) == FALSE) |>
  filter(Num_leaves != 0)

# Visual verification
SPAD_Data_no_NA

# Generating mixed effects model for SPAD value data with lmer(), using Block, Date, and Multiple_Seedling as random effects
SPAD_Model = lmer(
  SPAD_Value ~ Treatment + (1|Block) + (1|Date) + (1|Multiple_Seedling),
  data = SPAD_Data_no_NA)

# Checking plot of residuals vs. fitted for our model with plot()
plot(SPAD_Model)
```

Our data does not have homogeneity of variance. We'll check it visually for outliers.

```{r}
# Visually checking data for outliers
SPAD_Data_no_NA
```

We cannot remove any outliers here, so we will compare sample sizes per treatment to see if they're comparable.

```{r}
# Generating count of values per treatment with summarise()
SPAD_Data_no_NA |>
  group_by(Treatment) |>
  summarise(n = n())
```

Our overall sample size is large and the individual sample size for each treatment is comparable, so we will hope the anova() command robustness will accommodate the heteroskedasticity.

```{r}
# Checking normality in SPAD_Value using hist()
hist(SPAD_Data_no_NA$SPAD_Value)
```

It is not immediately clear if our data is sufficently normal, but the sample size is too large for a Shapiro-Wilk test to give reliable results. We will assume normality under the central limit theorem.

#### Conducting ANOVA Test

```{r}
# Displaying ANOVA table with anova()
SPAD_ANOVA = anova(SPAD_Model)
SPAD_ANOVA

# Saving ANOVA table with write.csv()
write.csv(SPAD_ANOVA, "SPAD_ANOVA.csv", row.names = FALSE)

# Conducting post-hoc test with emmeans() to fit the lmer() model, using Tukey adjustment
emmeans(SPAD_Model, pairwise ~ Treatment, adjust = "Tukey")
```

Our ANOVA table shows significant differences found among treatments (p = 0.0002576), identified as AC - DT (p = 0.0116) and AC - OS (p = 0.0010) after a Tukey post-hoc test.

#### Checking Prerequisites for ANOVA Testing

```{r}
# Creating backup tibble with dead seedlings removed, using filter()
Height_Data_Alive = Height_Data_Clean |>
  filter(Seedling_Ht_cm > 0)

# Visual verification
Height_Data_Alive

# Generating mixed effects model for seedling height data with lmer(), using Block, Date, and Multiple_Seedling as random effects
Height_Model = lmer(
  Seedling_Ht_cm ~ Treatment + (1|Block) + (1|Date) + (1|Multiple_Seedling),
  data = Height_Data_Alive)

# Checking plot of residuals vs. fitted for our model with plot()
plot(Height_Model)
```

We can immediately see that there is not homogeneity of variance for our data. We will investigate visually.

```{r}
# Visually searching for outliers
Height_Data_Alive
```

We have no reason to remove any values here, so we will check counts for each treatment to see if they're comparable.

```{r}
# Generating count of values per treatment with summarise()
Height_Data_Alive |>
  group_by(Treatment) |>
  summarise(n = n())
```

We unfortunately lack any way to reliably account for heteroskedasticity, so we will have to hope the small unevenness in variation means anova() will be robust enough to handle it.

```{r}
# Checking histogram of Seedling_Ht_cm with hist() to check for normality
hist(Height_Data_Alive$Seedling_Ht_cm, breaks = 10)
```

Our data has a tail but appears mostly normal, with this assumption being supported by the central limit theorem. We will proceed with a multiple-effects ANOVA.

#### Conducting ANOVA Test

```{r}
# Displaying ANOVA table with anova()
Height_ANOVA = anova(Height_Model)
Height_ANOVA

# Saving ANOVA table with read.csv()
write.csv(Height_ANOVA, "Height_ANOVA.csv", row.names = FALSE)

# Conducting post-hoc test with emmeans() to fit the lmer() model, using Tukey adjustment
emmeans(Height_Model, pairwise ~ Treatment, adjust = "Tukey")
```

Our ANOVA table shows significant differences found amongs treatments (p = 1.743e-07), identified as AC - OS (p = 0.0001) and DT-OS (p \< 0.0001) after a Tukey post-hoc test.

#### Visualizing ANOVA Results

```{r}
# Visualizing mean seedling heights with ANOVA results added
Height_Data_Alive |>

  # Calculating summary statistics with summarise()
  group_by(Treatment) |>
  summarise(
    mean_Height = mean(Seedling_Ht_cm),
    sd_Height = sd(Seedling_Ht_cm),
    n = n(),
    se_Height = sd_Height/sqrt(n)
  ) |>
  
  # Generating column plot with error bars using ggplot() + geom_col() +
  # geom_errorbar()
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = Treatment, y = mean_Height) +
  geom_col(color = "black", fill= NA) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(
    ymin = mean_Height - se_Height,
    ymax = mean_Height + se_Height
  ),
  position = position_dodge(0.9), width = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_text(
    label = c("", "", "B"),
    vjust = 6, size = 6, family = "serif"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    label = c("A", "A", ""),
    vjust = 3, size = 6, family = "serif"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    label = c("F = 25.836\ndf1 = 2\ndf2 = 33.091\np = 1.743e-07"),
    x = 1, y = 40, size = 12, size.unit = "pt", family = "serif"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = 12, family = "serif"),
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Treatment",
    y = "Seedling Height (in cm)"
  )

# Saving plot with ggsave()
ggsave("Height_ANOVA_Plot.png", path = "Plots", units = "in", width = 5.5, 
  height = 3.75, dpi = 300)
```

Column plot of mean seedling height between treatments, with standard error bars depicted at the top of each column. Results from a one-way ANOVA are denoted within each column. The open sky treatment was found to differ from the adult canopy (p = 0.0001) and dead tree (p \< 0.0001) treatments.

## 2.7. Evaluating Leaf Count by Treatment

#### Initial Visualization of Leaf Count by Treatment

```{r}
# Creating visualization of mean leaf count value for each treatment
SPAD_Data_Clean |>
  
  # Removing plants without leaves and NA SPAD values using filter() to remain
  # consistent with our previous ANOVA testing on SPAD data 
  filter(Num_leaves > 0) |>
  filter(is.na(SPAD_Value) == FALSE) |>
  
  # Generating summary statistics with summarise()
  group_by(Treatment) |>
  summarise(
    mean_Leaf = mean(Num_leaves),
    sd_Leaf = sd(Num_leaves),
    n = n(),
    se_Leaf = sd_Leaf/sqrt(n)
  ) |>
  
  # Creating column plot with error bars using ggplot() + geom_bar() +
  # geom_errorbar()
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = Treatment, y = mean_Leaf) +
  geom_col(color = "black", fill = NA) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(
    ymin = mean_Leaf - se_Leaf,
    ymax = mean_Leaf + se_Leaf
  ),
  position = position_dodge(0.9), width = 0.2
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = 12, family = "serif"),
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Treatment",
    y = "Leaf Count (# of individual leaves)"
  )
```

Column plot of mean leaf count at each treatment, with standard error bars visualized at the top of each column. The Natural Recruit treatment has a noticeably higher mean than all other treatments, with Open Sky lagging behind. Notably, the Adult Canopy treatment and Dead Tree treatment are equivalent here as observed in previous ANOVA tests on SPAD value and seedling height, with standard error for the other two treatments not being quite as high as it was for mean seedling heights.

#### Checking Prerequisites for ANOVA testing

Conveniently, we can reuse our SPAD data set copy from the SPAD ANOVA tests since it still retains data on leaf count. We will need to thin our leaf counts as done in our regression testing on leaf count, however.

```{r}
# Removing duplicated leaf count values with distinct()
Leaf_Model_Data = SPAD_Data_no_NA |>
  group_by(ID_num, Sapling_Num) |>
  distinct(Num_leaves, .keep_all = TRUE)

# Generating mixed effects model for leaf count data with lmer(), using Block, Date, and Multiple_Seedling as random effects
Leaf_Model = lmer(
  Num_leaves ~ Treatment + (1|Block) + (1|Date) + (1|Multiple_Seedling),
  data = Leaf_Model_Data)

# Checking residuals vs. fitted plot with plot()
plot(Leaf_Model)
```

While this has reduced noise in our data, there is a colossal outlier skewing our data. We will visually investigate.

```{r}
# Visually checking for outliers
Leaf_Model_Data
```

Our outlier is the large OS treatment outlier observed earlier. We will remove this, noting its removal in our final figure, and re-draw our model.

```{r}
# Removing outliers with filter()
Leaf_Model_Data = Leaf_Model_Data |>
  filter(Num_leaves < 100)

# Visual verification
Leaf_Model_Data

# Generating mixed effects model for leaf count data with lmer(), using Block, Date, and Multiple_Seedling as random effects
Leaf_Model = lmer(
  Num_leaves ~ Treatment + (1|Block) + (1|Date) + (1|Multiple_Seedling),
  data = Leaf_Model_Data)

# Checking residuals vs. fitted plot with plot()
plot(Leaf_Model)

# Viewing histogram of leaf counts with hist() to check for normality
hist(Leaf_Model_Data$Num_leaves, breaks = 10)
```

While our data is skewed slightly to the left, we can assume normality via the central limit theorem since our sample size is over 30 (n = 56).

#### Conducting ANOVA Test

```{r}
# Viewing ANOVA table with anova()
Leaf_ANOVA = anova(Leaf_Model)
Leaf_ANOVA

# Saving ANOVA table with write.csv()
write.csv(Leaf_ANOVA, "Leaf_ANOVA.csv", row.names = FALSE)

# Conducting post-hoc test with emmeans() to fit the lmer() model, using Tukey adjustment
emmeans(Leaf_Model, pairwise ~ Treatment, adjust = "Tukey")
```

Our ANOVA table shows significant differences found among treatments (p = 1.719e-06), identified as AC - OS (p \< 0.0001) and DT - OS (p = 0.0002) after a Tukey post-hoc test.

#### Visualizing ANOVA Results

```{r}

  ) |>

  ggplot() +
```

Column plot of mean leaf count between treatments, with standard error bars depicted at the top of each column. Results from a one-way ANOVA are denoted within each column.
